paragraphs.heading: Life at the edges
paragraphs.text: An extremophile is a living thing that can live, or even thrive, in extreme conditions: great heat or cold, high pressure, strong radiation, heavy salt, or extreme pH, a measure of acidity. Most are microbes, both bacteria and, above all, archaea, though some fungi and other eukaryotes count too. Surviving is not the same as thriving, however. Tolerant or resistant organisms may simply hold on in harsh places, so the very tough tardigrade is not strictly an extremophile.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: What counts as extreme is judged against an arbitrary standard, often a human one. Seen that way, extremophiles can be considered ecologically dominant across the planet's history, and they remain among the most abundant forms of life. Studying them has widened what we know about the limits of life and feeds ideas about life beyond Earth. They might also help clean up places that pollution or contamination has made hazardous to people.

paragraphs.heading: Where they turn up
paragraphs.text: In the 1980s and 1990s, biologists found microbes living in acidic, very hot or irregular-pressure niches that complex organisms could not bear. Some scientists even concluded that life may have begun at hydrothermal vents deep under the ocean. Bacteria have been found in a lake buried half a mile under Antarctic ice and in the Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the oceans. Ocean expeditions found microbes in 120 °C sediment 1.2 km below the seafloor in the Nankai Trough, and others thriving in rocks up to 580 m below the sea floor off the northwestern United States.

paragraphs.heading: Named for what they like
paragraphs.text: Each kind of extremophile is named for the condition it grows best in. Acidophiles prefer a pH of 3.0 or below, and alkaliphiles a pH of 9.0 or above. Halophiles grow best in at least 50 g/L of dissolved salt, against roughly 35 g/L on a coral reef. Thermophiles prefer temperatures above 45 °C, hyperthermophiles above 80 °C, and psychrophiles 15 °C or lower. Piezophiles grow best at pressures above 10 MPa.

paragraphs.heading: More than one extreme
paragraphs.text: These labels are not exclusive, and organisms that fit several are called polyextremophiles. Microbes living in hot rocks deep underground, such as Thermococcus barophilus, are both thermophiles and piezophiles. One living on a mountaintop in the Atacama Desert might be radioresistant, a xerophile that grows best when water activity is below 0.8, a psychrophile, and an oligotroph that grows best where nutrients are scarce.

paragraphs.heading: Built to cope
paragraphs.text: Part of how extremophiles adapt lies in the amino acids that make up their proteins, which affect how those proteins fold under particular conditions. Some can take remarkable punishment. Tom Gheysens of Ghent University in Belgium and colleagues found that endospores of a Bacillus species were still viable after being heated to 420 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Clues for other worlds
paragraphs.text: Astrobiology studies how life arises, spreads and evolves in the universe, drawing on physics, chemistry, biology, geology and many other fields. Astrobiologists care about extremophiles because they let them map Earth's limits of life onto possible environments elsewhere. Deserts in Antarctica, for example, face harmful UV radiation, cold, high salt and few minerals, which makes them useful stand-ins.
